# Introduction

## Overview

- The **primary purpose** of the esophagus is **transport** of food from mouth to stomach  
- No digestive or absorptive function  
- Muscular tube from **cricoid cartilage** (C6) → traverses chest → ends in upper abdomen  

## Length & Segments

- Total length: **22–28 cm** (C6 to T11, gastroesophageal junction)  
- Varies with patient height  
- Esophageal bed lies in **posterior mediastinum** (shortest reconstruction route: ~30 cm)  

:::{.callout-note}
If orthotopic route unavailable:  
- Retrosternal: 32 cm  
- Subcutaneous: 34 cm  
:::

## Endoscopic Landmarks

| Landmark | Distance from incisors |
|----------|------------------------|
| Upper esophageal sphincter (UES) | ~15 cm |
| Carina | ~25 cm |
| LES (men) | 38–40 cm |
| LES (women) | 36–38 cm |

## Surgical Planning

- Tumor location relative to **carina** (25 cm) helps decide **left vs. right thoracotomy**  
- Avoid aortic arch (blocks left upper thoracic esophagus access)

## Anatomic Narrowings (3 areas)

1. **Cricopharyngeal** (UES) – narrowest part of GI tract (**1.5 cm** diameter)  
2. **Aortic arch / left mainstem bronchus / left atrium** – at ~22 cm from incisors  
3. **Lower esophageal sphincter**  

:::{.callout-warning}
Foreign bodies often lodge at these narrowings  
:::

## Esophageal Wall Layers

Four layers (inner to outer):

- **Mucosa** (squamous epithelium, lamina propria, muscularis mucosa)  
- **Submucosa**  
- **Muscularis propria** (inner circular + outer longitudinal)  
- **Adventitia** (no serosa)

## Laimer's Triangle

- Longitudinal muscle originates from cricoid as **two bundles**  
- Converge 3 cm distal to cricopharyngeus → leaves a **V‑shaped weak area** posteriorly  
- Covered only by circular fibers → **Laimer’s triangle**

## Muscle Type Transition

- **Upper 40%** of esophagus: striated muscle  
- Gradual transition → **smooth muscle** in distal two‑thirds  
- Motility disorders (e.g., achalasia) mainly affect **distal smooth muscle**  

---

# Cervical Esophagus

## Anatomy & Approach

- Length: **5 cm** (C6 to suprasternal notch)  
- Shifts to **left** at base of neck → best approach via **left neck incision**  
- Surrounded by loose fibroareolar tissue → no serosa, no mesentery

## Cervical Compartments

| Structure | Location |
|-----------|----------|
| Pretracheal fascia | Anterior (extends to pericardium) |
| Prevertebral fascia | Posterior (extends to diaphragm) |
| Carotid sheaths | Lateral |

- Paraesophageal space (anterior) & retroesophageal space (posterior)

## Clinical Danger: Descending Infections

- Tonsillar/dental abscesses → spread via these compartments into mediastinum  
- **Necrotizing mediastinitis** – requires early surgical drainage  
- Iatrogenic perforation most common **above cricopharyngeal narrowing** → posterior pharyngeal perforation

## Blood Supply – Cervical Esophagus

- Right & left **superior** and **inferior** thyroid arteries  
- Small branches from common carotid & subclavian arteries  
- Venous drainage: **inferior thyroid vein**

## Innervation

- **Recurrent laryngeal nerves**  
- **Sympathetic chains**

---

# Upper Esophageal Sphincter (UES)

## Muscular Components

- Three bilateral constrictor muscles (inferior, middle, superior)  
- **Cricopharyngeal muscle** – continuous band from cricoid cartilage  
- Blends with inferior pharyngeal constrictor & circular esophageal muscle

## Killian’s Triangle

- Weak area **between** inferior constrictor and cricopharyngeal muscle  
- **Zenker’s (pulsion) diverticulum** can form here  
- Associated with cricopharyngeal hypertrophy or dysmotility

## UES Function

- High‑pressure zone: **2–4 cm**  
- Mixture of fast‑ & slow‑twitch **striated** fibers → basal tone + rapid changes for swallowing  
- Relaxes as intrapharyngeal pressure increases → food bolus enters cervical esophagus

---

# Recurrent Laryngeal Nerves (RLN)

## Origin & Course

- Originate from **vagus nerves**  
- **Right RLN**: recurs around **right subclavian artery**  
- **Left RLN**: recurs around **aortic arch**  
- Both ascend in **tracheoesophageal groove** (left nerve closer to esophagus)

## Non‑recurrent Nerve

- Rare on right side: incidence **0.1%** (Toniato et al.)  
- Never on left

## Injury Prevention & Consequences

- During transhiatal esophagectomy or Zenker’s diverticulectomy:  
  - Sharply dissect fat off esophagus  
  - Retract trachea **gently with finger** (no metal retractors)  
- Injury → **hoarseness**, impaired swallowing, aspiration risk  
- Bilateral injury → **airway obstruction**,可能需要 tracheostomy  
- Experienced surgeon incidence: ~1%

---

# Thoracic Esophagus

## Length & Course

- Length: **20 cm** (thoracic inlet → diaphragmatic hiatus)  
- Shifts to **right** at T7 → best approach: **right thoracotomy** (e.g., Ivor Lewis)  
- Distal thoracic esophagus angulates left after hiatus → best approach for hiatal hernia/epiphrenic diverticulum: **left**

## Arterial Blood Supply

- **Bronchial arteries** (1 right‑sided, 1–2 left‑sided)  
- Usually **2 esophageal branches** from descending aorta (T6–T9)  
- Rich intramural collateral network → esophagus can be mobilized extensively yet remain perfused

## Venous Drainage

- Primarily **azygos vein**  
- Also hemiazygos & bronchial veins

## Relations – Upper Thorax

| Structure | Position |
|-----------|----------|
| Trachea | Anterior |
| Azygos vein | Right side |
| Left subclavian artery & aortic arch | Left side |

- Descending aorta posterior to left of esophagus until T8, then esophagus moves anterior to aorta

## Lower Thorax Relations

- **Pericardium & left atrium** lie anterior to esophagus  
- Locally advanced cancer invading heart/aorta = unresectable  
- Aortoesophageal fistula → **sentinel hematemesis** (fatal exsanguination if missed)  
- Posterior: spine (T8 → esophagus moves anteriorly)

## Boerhaave’s Perforation

- Left lateral distal esophagus covered only by mediastinal pleura → weakest area  
- **Spontaneous perforation** most common along left lateral aspect

---

# Vagus Nerves (Thoracic)

## Course & Branches

- RLN branches given off (already covered)  
- Vagal & sympathetic fibers form **myenteric (Auerbach’s) plexus** → controls peristalsis  
- **Submucosal (Meissner’s) plexus** → muscularis mucosae & secretions  

## Achalasia

- Degeneration of Auerbach’s plexus ganglion → aperistalsis + impaired LES relaxation

## Distal Esophagus

- At tracheal bifurcation → pulmonary & esophageal plexuses  
- Anterior vagus (from left vagus) and **posterior vagal trunk** (from right vagus)  
- Both trunks pass through hiatus with esophagus

---

# Azygos Vein & Esophageal Exposure

- Adjacent and to the **right** of upper thoracic esophagus  
- Can be involved by mid‑esophageal tumors  
- During transhiatal esophagectomy: avoid avulsion  
- Often **divided** during Ivor Lewis esophagectomy to improve exposure

---

# Lymphatic Drainage & Thoracic Duct

## Submucosal Lymphatic Network

- Rich network → allows **longitudinal spread** of tumor cells  
- **T1a** (mucosa only): nodal spread **2.6%**  
- **T1b** (invades submucosa): **22.2%**  
- **T2**: 43.2%  |  **T3**: 77.2%  |  **T4**: 66.7%

## Direction of Flow

- Above tracheal bifurcation → drains **superiorly** (paratracheal, subcarinal, paraesophageal)  
- Below carina → drains **inferiorly** (lower mediastinal, celiac, left gastric)  
- Blocked lymphatics can reverse flow (e.g., distal tumor found in proximal esophagus)

## Thoracic Duct

- Begins as **cisterna chyli** (T12)  
- Lies on vertebral bodies, posterior to esophagus, between azygos (right) and aorta (left)  
- Turns behind left mainstem bronchus (T5–T6) → empties into left subclavian/jugular junction  

## Chylothorax

- Damage in 1–2% of esophagectomies  
- High pink/clear chest output → becomes **milky** after dietary fat  
- Treatment: surgical ligation or interventional radiology embolization

---

# Abdominal Esophagus

## Length & Relations

- Normal length: **3–6 cm**  
- Angulates to **left** after passing diaphragmatic hiatus  
- Ends at **cardia** along lesser curvature  

## Blood Supply

- Small arteries from **left gastric artery** & **inferior phrenic artery**  
- Venous drainage: **left gastric vein**  
- Subepithelial venous plexus in lamina propria → connects to portal system → **esophageal varices**

## Regional Lymph Nodes (Abdomen)

- Stations: 15 (diaphragmatic), 16 (paracardial), 17 (left gastric), 18 (common hepatic), 19 (splenic), 20 (celiac)

## Esophageal Hiatus

- At T10 level  
- Crura originate from L1–L4 vertebrae  
- Left lobe of liver anteriorly (divide triangular ligament for exposure)  
- Aorta passes through its own hiatus (bordered by **median arcuate ligament** – used in Hill repair)

---

# Vagus Nerves at Hiatus

- **Anterior vagus** – usually adjacent to esophageal wall  
- **Posterior vagus** – may be further away  
- Identify both during Nissen fundoplication / hiatal hernia repair  
- Injury → delayed gastric emptying in ~15% of patients

---

# Diaphragm & Phrenoesophageal Membrane (PEM)

## PEM Structure

- Also called Laimer’s or Allison’s membrane  
- Two sheaths:  
  1. Superior sheath (2–4 cm along distal esophagus → inserts into submucosa)  
  2. Inferior sheath (across cardia → gastric serosa, dorsal mesentery, gastrohepatic ligament)  
- Allows dynamic movement of esophagus relative to diaphragm

## Crura & Anti‑reflux

- **Right crus** (deep & superficial layers) forms most of esophageal hiatus  
- Left crus forms one edge of aortic hiatus  
- Crura contribute to extrinsic sphincter function

---

# Gastroesophageal Reflux Barrier

## Components

1. **Intrinsic LES** (smooth muscle clasp & sling fibers)  
2. **Extrinsic** – diaphragmatic crura + PEM attachments  
3. Intra‑abdominal pressure gradient  

- Obesity, pregnancy, gastroparesis → higher intragastric pressure → more reflux  
- Weight loss reduces reflux

## Definition of GEJ (controversial)

| Criterion | Definition |
|-----------|------------|
| Histologic | End of submucosal esophageal glands / start of oxyntic glands |
| Endoscopic | Squamocolumnar junction (Z‑line) / proximal gastric folds |
| Surgical | Peritoneal reflection / junction of tubular esophagus & stomach |

:::{.callout-tip}
Remove gastric fat pad during Nissen or Heller to accurately identify GEJ  
:::

---

# Lower Esophageal Sphincter (LES)

## Muscular Architecture

- Circular muscle thickens ~3 cm proximal to GEJ  
- Along **lesser curvature**: short **clasp fibers**  
- Along greater curvature & angle of His: **oblique gastric sling fibers**  
- High‑pressure zone extends 3–4 cm above GEJ + 1–2 cm onto stomach  

## LES Pressure

- Resting pressure: **10–30 mmHg**  
- Relaxes ~3 seconds after swallowing  
- Hypotensive LES → nocturnal/postprandial reflux

## Asymmetry

- Manometry shows **radial & axial asymmetry**  
- Highest pressure & shortest length toward **greater curvature** (Mittal et al., 2017)

## Reflux Mechanisms

- Transient LES relaxation (most common)  
- Low basal LES pressure  
- Swallow‑associated relaxation  
- Straining (e.g., increased abdominal pressure)

---

# Diaphragmatic Crura & Reflux

- Crura act as **external sphincter**  
- Pressure varies with respiration  
- During increased intra‑abdominal pressure (coughing, straining) → crura compress esophagus → prevent reflux

---

# Hiatal Hernia

## Pathogenesis

- Aging → elastic fibers of PEM replaced by inelastic tissue  
- Abnormal anchorage + adipose tissue between PEM and cardia  

## Classification (4 types)

| Type | Name | Features |
|------|------|----------|
| I | Sliding | GEJ above diaphragm, stomach partially herniated |
| II | Pure paraesophageal | GEJ fixed at hiatus, fundus herniated |
| III | Combined | Cardia above diaphragm + fundus herniated along esophagus |
| IV | Complex | Stomach + colon, small bowel, or spleen herniated |

## Clinical Consequences

- Disrupts crural sphincter function  
- Displaces LES away from crura  
- Gastric fluid trapped above hiatus → re‑reflux (impaired clearance)  
- Larger hernias → more acid reflux, lower LES pressure, weaker peristalsis, severe esophagitis

---

# Summary of Surgical Approaches

| Esophageal segment | Preferred approach |
|--------------------|-------------------|
| Cervical | Left neck incision |
| Mid‑thoracic | Right thoracotomy (e.g., Ivor Lewis) |
| Distal thoracic / hiatus | Left thoracotomy (hiatal hernia, epiphrenic diverticulum) |
| Abdominal | Laparotomy / laparoscopy |

---

# Key Clinical Correlations

- **Aortoesophageal fistula** – sentinel hematemesis, fatal if not recognized  
- **Tracheoesophageal fistula** – avoid dissection injury to membranous trachea  
- **Spinal abscess** – from cervical perforation/anastomotic leak  
- **Chylothorax** – milky chest tube output after feeding  
- **Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury** – hoarseness, aspiration  

---

# Conclusion

- The esophagus is a **muscular tube** (transport, no digestion)  
- **UES** and **LES** + **diaphragmatic crura** provide anti‑reflux barrier  
- Extensive **submucosal lymphatic & vascular networks** allow tumor spread and collateral perfusion  
- Detailed knowledge of **surrounding structures** (trachea, aorta, pleura, recurrent nerves, thoracic duct) is essential for safe surgery and prevention of complications
